card.name: Podaraki
card.tagline: A 10th-century Pontic Greek circle dance driven by heavy foot stomping.
card.profile: Podaraki is a traditional Greek dance originating in the Pontos region, dating back to the 10th century. Today, it is performed in modern-day Turkey and northern Thrace by both men and women. The name translates to "small foot" in Greek, reflecting the heavy foot stomping that characterizes the movement. Accompanying the dance is a female song where a protagonist calls young women to dance before marriage while critiquing domestic restrictions.
card.insight: Dating back to the 10th century, Podaraki translates to "small foot" yet features heavy foot stomping and defiant lyrics about marriage and revenge.
card.profile_long:
Podaraki is a historical Greek dance rooted in the Pontos region with documentation dating as far back as the 10th century. Over centuries of cultural continuity and geographic shift, the tradition has maintained its presence and is now actively performed in modern-day Turkey as well as the northern Thrace region. The name of the dance, Podaraki, translates from Greek as "small foot," an ironic descriptor given that the physical execution centers heavily on powerful stomping performed with the 'podia', or feet, of the dancers. As a social form, Podaraki is danced by both men and women. Participants typically join together in an open circle formation, with straight-line formations appearing only rarely.

The auditory foundation of Podaraki is tied to a specific female song known alternatively as 'mpate koritsia sto horo', which translates to "go girls to the dance." Lyrically, the song features a persona urging her peers to go out, dance, and embrace joy prior to entering marriage. As the song progresses into its second half, the thematic tone shifts into traditional social commentary. The protagonist voices sharp criticism directed at her husband, mother-in-law, and father-in-law for attempting to restrict her from dancing and seeking leisure. The narrative culminates as the singer details the methods she uses to exact revenge upon her husband, in-laws, and even her children for these constraints, blending playful rebellion with stark folk storytelling. Classified broadly under Greek folk dance traditions, Podaraki bridges ancient regional heritage with communal expression through its characteristic footwork and vocal accompaniment.

sections.origins_and_history: Podaraki is a Greek dance from the Pontos region, dating to the 10th century. It is now danced in modern-day Turkey as well as the northern Thrace.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is called Podaraki because it involves much stomping with the Podia (feet) of the dancer. It is danced both by men and women usually in an open circle, and rarely in straight line.
sections.music_and_instruments: It is a female song, also called μπάτε "κορίτσια στο χορό" (mpate koritsia sto horo), meaning "go girls to the dance." In the song, a supposed girl calls the other girls to go dancing and have fun before marrying.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: In its second half, after expressing the traditional criticism against both her husband and her mother and father-in-law for not letting her go dance and have fun, the supposed girl explains how she avenges both them and her children for that.
sections.regional_variants: It is danced in the Pontos region, modern-day Turkey, and northern Thrace.
